The NHI Bill - can it deliver universal health care for South Africans?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This month the National Health Insurance Bill was introduced to Parliament, but will NHI be able to address health care provision inequality given the reality of the economic challenges facing SA?

Unique Selling Point:
Whether it be by individuals, insurance schemes or government, over half of South African health care spending is on 16% of the population, a reflection of one glaring aspect of inequality that has been a dripping sore affecting post independence South Africa since 1994. A consensus exists that says this state of affairs is untenable, but what is the solution?

The NHI is the ANC government’s solution, the exact form of which is in development even though the Bill has already been tabled in parliament. Even so, the government has announced NHI will be in operation in 2026.

There have been localized, so-called pilots that in effect became restricted to limited learning exercises, because the infrastructure of the districts struggled to cope with the demands of the process (eg transport, lack of IT staff and low numbers of participating doctors). A lack of detail on research and the way forward has meant opposition groups have been filling in the gaps and the public have been receiving confused messages.

But in reality NHI is already here whatever form it takes. So what happens between now and 2026 for patients, GPs, dentists etc.? Are the plans and timetable for the plans cast in stone? Are there other options being explored? How different might the situation look after the completion of public participation stages?

As NHI starts up, we get a grip on the current operations of the project, the fiscal implications for our nation and citizens, and the prospects for the medical industry. Fundamentally, if South Africa is to implement a viable system of fair, universal health care, then it is critical, whatever happens, that the country gets it right.

Summary:
So, if someone is now paying, say R 3500 for Medical Aid, and they know what they're covered for, what will be the difference under the NHI scheme? What services will they be eligible for, what will the personal cost to them be (eg. personal tax increase) and will there be clarity as to what treatments they're covered for?

The current preponderance of private medical aids has, according to industry insiders, led to a milking of the system and their members’ pockets, with over charging and over provision of medication and procedures. On the other hand there has been the well documented culture of widespread state corruption when it comes to state owned enterprises. So is the risk that the latter may replace the former, in reforming the public health apparatus, worth paying?

Further information:
Initial attention has been focussed on negative impacts on patients and practitioners currently in the private sector. These include:
- Possible future costs of Medical Aids - less premium payers, because people are relying on NHI and lower array of services offered by Medical Aids as a supplementary system, will mean private cover less substantive and more expensive.
- Specialists – the threat of another brain drain if specialists have to work longer hours for lower NHI tariffs to keep their standard of living / rewards.

Given that behind the scenes, officials are saying that the NHI will be decades in the making, it appears that we do have time to get it right. Given this, will the naysayers be won over if the government varies its strategy of implementation? If during the process, as the Health Minister has alluded to, the intensity of state corruption lessens (under increased scrutiny) so that state governance becomes much more trust-worthy, will that bring everyone together behind this ambitious project? Or will it all boil down to the fitness of the South African economy to deliver?

Note: we still have to find an expert on governance that isn’t Professor Alex van den Heefer of Wits School of Governance.

Press Release:


The National Health Insurance bill has been introduced to Parliament – bringing it a step closer to reality. But what will the NHI really mean for South African taxpayers?

Script:


LINK: As South Africans, we can all agree that medical care is expensive. If you’re on a private scheme it’s getting even harder to afford and about 85% of the population depends on a crumbling and inadequate public health system. Can the National Health Insurance Bill, a seeming reality by 2026 – be the cure all?

VO: According to Dr Nicholas Crisp, it can be. He's taken on the mammoth task of setting up the NHI's administrative and operational capacity for the Department of Health, in what will become the hub for South Africa's health care solutions.

Mac :The bill has been drafted it's been presented before parliament but it also covers a lot of criticism. Do you feel like you've been handed a hot potato.

Nicholas: Look any major reform of any description is bound to have opponents it's bound to raise anxiety. There's a lot of suspicion of things the government have done. But a hot potato, No this is something that I've been wanting to be involved in since the late 80s and I'm very excited we've got to this point.


VO: Russel Rensburg, Director of the Rural Health Advocacy Project believes that universal health care is a necessity, especially for 38% of South Africans who currently have difficulty in accessing medical care.

Russell: You know how many kids sit in the classroom and theyre made to feel stupid because nobody tested the eyesight. Now we have a school outreach scheme which will come to test you for your eyesight and within two or three weeks you have access to a pair of spectacles and your whole development trajectory changes health is a foundational element to broader human development.

VO: Topographical challenges in outlying areas, inhibit access to quality medical care and 95% of people in rural areas don't have medical aid.

Russell: What we liked about the NHI was a number of different things.It creates another formula that looks around what are the health needs of those particular populations. If this is too many young women what access how much money is there for reproductive health services. For us it looked like a better way to fund health care.

VO: This year the Department of Health estimates, that around 222 billion rand will be spent on public health care and approximately 250 billion rand in the private sector which only serves about 15% of South Africans
According to Dr Anban Pillay, Deputy Director General for the NHI, The Bill proposes to aggregate these funds into one large pool.


Anban: We think we can spend less than 480 billion and give everybody a great package of services relative to what they are paying now and for them to pay less for those services.

VO: Dr Johann Serfontein, consults to the South African Private Practitioners Forum. He emphasises that at the current economic growth of 0.6% these funds will not be adequate.

Johann: The Davis Tax Commission report in 2017 indicated that unless South Africa has significant economic growth sustainable year on year of at least 5 percent there is no way that we can implement universal health coverage.

VO: Government says there is money available. Over and above the current health budget, by 2026 NHI will be funded through a combination of taxes: general tax, a surcharge on personal income tax, payroll tax and a redistribution of medical scheme tax credits.//

But estimates by economists of how much funding is required to implement NHI annually, in actual rands and cents, are wide ranging.







Anban: They even have raised figures of 800 billion. And all of these figures are based on the assumption of the cost in the private health sector currently. What people have not done is recosted the model based on the way we have proposed it.

Nicholas: At the moment the way in which the fee structure works in the private sector is on a fee for service so you get an itemized bill from your medical aid. So by listing five or six different codes the patient will not know except for if you're a health practitioner whether those codes are justified or unjustified.

VO: The way the rest of the world is moving to decrease overall medical costs, is to pay for the outcome, like a hip replacement, not individual items for example the suture or plaster that tend to drive the costs up, and the NHI plans to do the same.

Nicholas: Let me give you an example. A relative recently was quoted 33000 Rand for a dental procedure which involved removing two teeth and doing a whole host of itemized things on this bill. There's no way I was going to accept this itemized quote for this procedure and asked a dentist whom I trust to give me an opinion on the quote without going into the details the procedure was done finished for 1800 Rand by the dentist.
Mac: No ways!

Johann: One of the mechanisms that is there is for hospitals to be paid what they call a DRG diagnosis related groups which is like a lump sum for a patient to get treated for a specific condition. It implies that the doctors working on this patient are also employed by the hospital and doctors don't want to be employed by hospitals. because the hospital starts putting pressure on you to practice in a specific way.

LINK: Many aspects of the NHI remain unclear, especially for the private medical industry . One of the main fears amongst specialist doctors is the uncertainty of tariffs and operational cost issues.// The threat is they may choose to just close shop and head for greener pastures.

Nicholas: if you did rapidly just cut somebody's income off in the next month then that is a result you're going to get. So that's obviously not the responsible way to do it.

Johann: Healthcare professionals want to work in an environment where if you set up a practice today which is very costly you know that 10 years from now you'll be able to cover your practice costs.

VO: The NHI aims to shift certain services, So first you would visit a primary health care practitioner, like a GP who would then only refer you to a specialist if necessary.

Nicholas: And so you push the cost down and you make the highly specialized people more available to see to the genuine problems.


VO: What makes the NHI's funding model feasible according to the Department of Health, is economies of scale. So if everyone comes into the pool, then the NHI pays less for services including medications.

Anban: You will access services based on your clinical needs, in other words next year I'm very sick and I need to see the doctor very often but year after maybe I wouldn't see him once.

VO: So who will be in charge of the Billions in the NHI coffers? The Minister of Health of course, who in turn will appoint 11 board members to oversee the entire NHI entity.

Tendai Mafuna is a legal researcher for Section 27 that advocates access to health care services. They support the NHI and have been monitoring the bill since its inception

Tendai: The amount of power that is given to the Minister is quite a lot of power and we just think that there is a lot of room for political interference because there's not a lot of oversight from other independent bodies such as the parliamentary committees.

Anban: The National Health Insurance fund is what we call a section 3 public entity. So it must have a board it must have a CEO. Why is the Minister appointing these people. Well the minister is effectively like the CEO of the health system.

Mac: Remember that that's what happened at Eskom and SABC, so that doesn't necessarily give people comfort.

Anban: the board members before appointment must be interviewed by an independent panel and publicly interview so everybody can understand who are the potential candidates and have a sight of what the shortlist would look like.

Tendai: The bill really just makes provision for accountability at a very high level. We should also just be looking at the health system in general to see where have we been failing in terms of governance and accountability and transparency

LINK: It is foreseen that medical aids as we know them may no longer exist,// he bill proposes that Medical aids will provide complementary services not covered by the NHI. That's the theory at least......

Nicholas: Whatever is covered by the full package of the NHI may not be included in a medical scheme. Anything that is an exclusion that is what medical insurance or medical schemes will be allowed to cover for top up or you can pay for it cash

Johann: It could also mean a service rendered by a private practitioner who isn't contracted of the fund would also not be paid for by the NHI Fund and the medical scheme may be able to cover that as well.

VO: When it comes to exclusions in the NHI, illegal immigrants and asylum seekers will be worse off, they will only be eligible for emergency care and services relating to notifiable diseases such as TB.

Tendai: So currently everyone in South Africa is able to access HIV treatment if they need it regardless of their status. even though we are acknowledging that the resources are limited we still really need to think about the public health benefit.

VO: The public participation phase is on, so now is the time for South Africans to have a say.

LINK: Although there are many public health facilities that are centres of medical excellence, other hospitals are in desperate need of urgent attention. Under the NHI, only those that comply can service the system.

Nicholas: The purpose of complying is to make sure that we systematically improve the quality of what happens in the facilities. That includes the physical quality of the building, the clinical quality, medicine availability everything.

Mac: 2026 is the year that everything is supposed to come together. Do you see that happening?
Johann: I don't think realistically we can expect anything of this nature before 2056. I think there is just too much that needs to happen there's too much uncertainty.
VO: But Dr Nicholas Crisp, is a man with a purpose.
Nicholas: We will set up the nucleus of the office by January next year. We hope by the time we have the administrative and operations in place - that people like me will be able to leave our medical aid knowing that we can get good healthcare in the new NHI system in five years time.

Anban: The National Health Insurance fund is what we call a section 3 public entity. So it must have a board it must have a CEO. Why is the Minister appointing these people. Well the minister is effectively like the CEO of the health system. Mac: Remember that that's what happened at Eskom and SABC, so that doesn't necessarily give people comfort. Anban: the board members before appointment must be interviewed by an independent panel and publicly interview so everybody can understand who are the potential candidates and have a sight of what the shortlist would look like. Tendai: The bill really just makes provision for accountability at a very high level. We should also just be looking at the health system in general to see where have we been failing in terms of governance and accountability and transparency LINK: It is foreseen that medical aids as we know them may no longer exist,// he bill proposes that Medical aids will provide complementary services not covered by the NHI. That's the theory at least...... Nicholas: Whatever is covered by the full package of the NHI may not be included in a medical scheme. Anything that is an exclusion that is what medical insurance or medical schemes will be allowed to cover for top up or you can pay for it cash Johann: It could also mean a service rendered by a private practitioner who isn't contracted of the fund would also not be paid for by the NHI Fund and the medical scheme may be able to cover that as well. VO: When it comes to exclusions in the NHI, illegal immigrants and asylum seekers will be worse off, they will only be eligible for emergency care and services relating to notifiable diseases such as TB. Tendai: So currently everyone in South Africa is able to access HIV treatment if they need it regardless of their status. even though we are acknowledging that the resources are limited we still really need to think about the public health benefit. VO: The public participation phase is on, so now is the time for South Africans to have a say. LINK: Although there are many public health facilities that are centres of medical excellence, other hospitals are in desperate need of urgent attention. Under the NHI, only those that comply can service the system. Nicholas: The purpose of complying is to make sure that we systematically improve the quality of what happens in the facilities. That includes the physical quality of the building, the clinical quality, medicine availability everything. Mac: 2026 is the year that everything is supposed to come together. Do you see that happening? Johann: I don't think realistically we can expect anything of this nature before 2056. I think there is just too much that needs to happen there's too much uncertainty. VO: But Dr Nicholas Crisp, is a man with a purpose. Nicholas: We will set up the nucleus of the office by January next year. We hope by the time we have the administrative and operations in place - that people like me will be able to leave our medical aid knowing that we can get good healthcare in the new NHI system in five years time.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): This month the National Health Insurance Bill was introduced to Parliament, but will NHI be able to address health care provision inequality given the reality of the economic challenges facing SA?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Whether it be by individuals, insurance schemes or government, over half of South African health care spending is on 16% of the population, a reflection of one glaring aspect of inequality that has been a dripping sore affecting post independence South Africa since 1994. A consensus exists that says this state of affairs is untenable, but what is the solution? The NHI is the ANC government’s solution, the exact form of which is in development even though the Bill has already been tabled in parliament. Even so, the government has announced NHI will be in operation in 2026. There have been localized, so-called pilots that in effect became restricted to limited learning exercises, because the infrastructure of the districts struggled to cope with the demands of the process (eg transport, lack of IT staff and low numbers of participating doctors). A lack of detail on research and the way forward has meant opposition groups have been filling in the gaps and the public have been receiving confused messages. But in reality NHI is already here whatever form it takes. So what happens between now and 2026 for patients, GPs, dentists etc.? Are the plans and timetable for the plans cast in stone? Are there other options being explored? How different might the situation look after the completion of public participation stages? As NHI starts up, we get a grip on the current operations of the project, the fiscal implications for our nation and citizens, and the prospects for the medical industry. Fundamentally, if South Africa is to implement a viable system of fair, universal health care, then it is critical, whatever happens, that the country gets it right.
metadata.Summary: So, if someone is now paying, say R 3500 for Medical Aid, and they know what they're covered for, what will be the difference under the NHI scheme? What services will they be eligible for, what will the personal cost to them be (eg. personal tax increase) and will there be clarity as to what treatments they're covered for? The current preponderance of private medical aids has, according to industry insiders, led to a milking of the system and their members’ pockets, with over charging and over provision of medication and procedures. On the other hand there has been the well documented culture of widespread state corruption when it comes to state owned enterprises. So is the risk that the latter may replace the former, in reforming the public health apparatus, worth paying?
metadata.Further information: Initial attention has been focussed on negative impacts on patients and practitioners currently in the private sector. These include: - Possible future costs of Medical Aids - less premium payers, because people are relying on NHI and lower array of services offered by Medical Aids as a supplementary system, will mean private cover less substantive and more expensive. - Specialists – the threat of another brain drain if specialists have to work longer hours for lower NHI tariffs to keep their standard of living / rewards. Given that behind the scenes, officials are saying that the NHI will be decades in the making, it appears that we do have time to get it right. Given this, will the naysayers be won over if the government varies its strategy of implementation? If during the process, as the Health Minister has alluded to, the intensity of state corruption lessens (under increased scrutiny) so that state governance becomes much more trust-worthy, will that bring everyone together behind this ambitious project? Or will it all boil down to the fitness of the South African economy to deliver? Note: we still have to find an expert on governance that isn’t Professor Alex van den Heefer of Wits School of Governance.
